claim: Rats were trained on an audiomotor frequency recognition go/no-go task requiring them to nose poke to a single target tone (4 kHz) for food reward and withhold from responding to other non-target tones (0.5 to 32 kHz separated by one octave intervals).
source: We trained 15 rats on an audiomotor frequency recognition go/no-go task (Carcea et al., 2017; Froemke et al., 2013; King et al., 2016; Martins and Froemke, 2015) that required them to nose poke to a single target tone for food reward and withhold from responding to other non-target tones (Figure 1A). Tones were 100 ms in duration presented sequentially once every 5–8 s at 70 dB sound pressure level (SPL); the target tone was 4 kHz and non-target tones ranged from 0.5 to 32 kHz separated by one octave intervals.
evidence: The manuscript describes the behavioral training protocol with specific parameters including tone frequencies, durations, and presentation intervals.

claim: After training, rats had high hit rates to target tones (88 ± 7%) and low false alarm rates to non-targets (7 ± 5%), leading to high d' values.
source: After a few weeks of training, rats had high hit rates to target tones and low false alarm rates to non-targets, leading to high d' values (mean performance shown in Figure 1B; each individual rat included in this study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Behavioral performance data is presented showing quantitative measures of hit rates, false alarm rates, and d' values, with reference to Figure 1B showing mean performance.

claim: Task performance was impaired after muscimol infusion into auditory cortex (AC) (p=0.03).
source: We found that task performance was impaired if either of these regions was inactivated, although general motor functions, including motivation or ability to feed were not impaired (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; for AC p=0.03; for FR2 p=0.009 Student's paired two-tailed t-test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of behavioral performance before and after muscimol infusion with p-value reported.

claim: Task performance was impaired after muscimol infusion into frontal cortical area 2 (FR2) (p=0.009).
source: We found that task performance was impaired if either of these regions was inactivated, although general motor functions, including motivation or ability to feed were not impaired (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; for AC p=0.03; for FR2 p=0.009 Student's paired two-tailed t-test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of behavioral performance before and after muscimol infusion with p-value reported.

claim: 60% of recorded cells were non-classically responsive in that they were neither tone modulated nor ramping (64/103 AC cells and 43/74 FR2 cells).
source: However, 60% of recorded cells were non-classically responsive in that they were neither tone modulated nor ramping according to statistical criteria (Figure 1E and F; Figure 1—figure supplement 5; 64/103 AC cells and 43/74 FR2 cells from 15 animals had neither significant tone-modulated activity or ramping activity; pre and post-stimulus mean activity compared via subsampled bootstrapping and considered significant when p<0.05; ramping activity measured with linear regression and considered significant via subsampled bootstrapping when p<0.05 and r > 0.5; for overall population statistics see Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of recorded neurons with specific statistical criteria for classification as non-classically responsive.

claim: The ISI distribution and trial-averaged firing rate capture different spike train statistics.
source: These models clearly demonstrate that trial-averaged rate modulation can occur with or without corresponding differences in the ISI distributions and cells without apparent trial-averaged rate-modulation can nevertheless have distinct ISI distributions. Taken together, these examples demonstrate that the ISI distribution and trial-averaged firing rate capture different spike train statistics.
evidence: Model cells are presented demonstrating dissociation between ISI distributions and trial-averaged firing rates.

claim: Non-classically responsive cells in both AC and FR2 provided significant spike-timing-based information about stimulus category and behavioral choice.
source: We found that non-classically responsive cells in both AC and FR2 provided significant spike-timing-based information about each task variable (Figure 4A,B, red; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Decoding analysis applied to non-classically responsive cells showing significant information content.

claim: Neurons in FR2 were more informative about stimulus category than AC (pstim = 0.0013).
source: Surprisingly, neurons in FR2 were more informative about stimulus category than AC, and AC neurons were more informative about choice than stimulus category (Figure 4A, pAC = 0.016, pstim = 0.0013, Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided).
evidence: Statistical comparison of decoding performance between brain regions with reported p-value.

claim: AC neurons were more informative about choice than stimulus category (pAC = 0.016).
source: Surprisingly, neurons in FR2 were more informative about stimulus category than AC, and AC neurons were more informative about choice than stimulus category (Figure 4A, pAC = 0.016, pstim = 0.0013, Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided).
evidence: Statistical comparison of decoding performance for different task variables with reported p-value.

claim: Choice non-classically responsive cells in AC were as informative as choice classically responsive cells (p=0.32).
source: Both of these observations would not have been detected at the level of the PSTH, as most cells in AC were non-classically responsive for behavioral choice (no ramping activity, 91/103), yet our decoder revealed that these same cells were as informative as choice classically responsive cells (Figure 4C, p=0.32 Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided; red circles indicate cells non-classically responsive for both variables, dark-red cells are choice non-classically responsive, and black cells are classically responsive).
evidence: Statistical comparison of decoding performance between non-classically responsive and classically responsive cells.

claim: Sensory non-classically responsive cells in FR2 contained comparable stimulus information to sensory classically responsive cells (p=0.29).
source: Similarly, most cells in FR2 were sensory non-classically responsive (not tone modulated, 60/74), yet contained comparable stimulus information to sensory classically responsive cells (Figure 4D, p=0.29 Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided; red cells are non-classically responsive for both variables, dark-red cells are sensory non-classically responsive, black cells are classically responsive).
evidence: Statistical comparison of decoding performance between non-classically responsive and classically responsive cells.

claim: The ISI-based decoder generally outperformed the conventional rate-based decoder (stimulus decoding: pAC = 0.0001, pFR2 = 8 × 10−6; choice decoding: pAC = 0.0057, pFR2 = 0.02).
source: When applied to our dataset, the ISI-based decoder generally outperformed this conventional rate-based decoder confirming that ISIs capture information distinct from that of the firing rate (Figure 5B; Overall stimulus decoding performance: pAC = 0.0001, pFR2 = 8 × 10−6; Overall choice decoding performance pAC = 0.0057, pFR2 = 0.02, Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided).
evidence: Direct comparison of two decoding methods with statistical significance reported.

claim: Single trial decoding outcomes showed weak to no correlations between the ISI-based decoder and the conventional rate decoder (stimulus medians: AC = 0.10 FR2 = 0.11; choice medians: AC = 0.07, FR2 = 0.08).
source: Moreover, comparing single trial decoding outcomes demonstrated weak to no correlations between the ISI-based decoder and the conventional rate decoder, further underscoring that these two methods rely on different features of the spike train to decode (Figure 5C; stimulus medians: AC = 0.10 FR2 = 0.11; choice medians: AC = 0.07, FR2 = 0.08).
evidence: Matthews correlation coefficient analysis showing low correlation values between decoding methods.

claim: ISI distributions of non-classically responsive cells in the Rodgers and DeWeese dataset encoded the selection rule and were significantly more informative than classically responsive cells (pAC = 5 × 10−6, pPFC <0.0002).
source: Using our algorithm, we found that the ISI distributions of these cells encoded the selection rule and were significantly more informative than the classically responsive cells (Figure 6E, pAC = 5 × 10−6, pPFC <0.0002, Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided).
evidence: Application of the decoding algorithm to an independent dataset with statistical comparison.

claim: Analyzing ensembles of two to eight neurons in AC and FR2 significantly improved decoding for both variables in FR2 and stimulus decoding in AC (pAC stim=0.04, pFR2 stim=1×10−5, pAC choice= 0.29, pFR2 choice=7×10−5).
source: Analyzing ensembles of two to eight neurons in AC and FR2 significantly improved decoding for both variables in FR2 and stimulus decoding in AC (Figure 7B, pAC stim=0.04, pFR2 stim=1×10−5, pAC = 0.29, pFR2 choice=7×10−5, Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided).
evidence: Statistical comparison of ensemble decoding performance versus single neuron decoding.

claim: Ensembles of neurons in AC and FR2 predicted behavioral errors, with ensembles in AC predicting errors significantly better than those in FR2 (for three-member ensembles: p=1.2 × 10−5, for four-member ensembles: p=0.03).
source: However, when we examined single-trial performance with our algorithm, ensembles of neurons in AC and FR2 predicted behavioral errors (Figure 7C). In general, ensembles in AC predicted behavioral errors significantly better than those in FR2 (Figure 7C, for three-member ensembles: p=1.2 × 10−5, for four-member ensembles: p=0.03, Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided).
evidence: Analysis of error prediction performance with statistical comparison between brain regions.

claim: Decoding with an increasing number of non-classically responsive cells improved error prediction in both AC and FR2 (pAC = 0.013, pFR2 = 0.046).
source: Interestingly, decoding with an increasing number of non-classically responsive cells improved error prediction in both AC and FR2 (Figure 7D, (pAC = 0.013, pFR2 = 0.046, Welch's t-test).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing relationship between number of non-classically responsive cells and error prediction performance.

claim: In FR2, sensory non-classically responsive ensembles reached consensus rapidly after stimulus onset followed by divergence on correct trials (Δconsensus, t = 0 to 0.42 s, pSNR = 3.9 × 10−4).
source: In FR2, sensory non-classically responsive ensembles (ensembles in which at least two out of three cells were not tone-modulated) encode stimulus information using temporally-precise stimulus-related dynamics on correct trials. The stimulus representation of sensory non-classically responsive ensembles reached consensus rapidly after stimulus onset followed by divergence (Figure 8E, stimulus-aligned, solid line, Δconsensus, t = 0 to 0.42 s, pSNR = 3.9 × 10−4 Wilcoxon test with Bonferroni correction, two-sided).
evidence: Consensus analysis showing temporal dynamics with statistical significance.

claim: Choice non-classically responsive ensembles in both regions as well as choice classically responsive ensembles in FR2 each reached consensus within 500 ms of the behavioral response on correct trials (Δconsensus, t = −1.0 to 0.0 s, pCNR = 2.0 × 10−5, pCR = 0.12).
source: For choice-related activity, choice non-classically responsive ensembles in both regions as well as choice classically responsive ensembles in FR2 each reached consensus within 500 ms of the behavioral response (Figure 8E, response-aligned, Δconsensus, t = −1.0 to 0.0 s, pCNR = 2.0 × 10−5, pCR = 0.12 Wilcoxon test with Bonferroni correction, two-sided).
evidence: Consensus analysis showing temporal dynamics relative to behavioral response with statistical significance.

claim: On error trials, stimulus consensus dynamics decreased over the course of the trial whereas choice dynamics did not display a systematic increase (Δconsensus, correct trials vs. error trials, stimulus: pSNR = 0.007, pSR = 0.065, choice: pCNR = 0.0048, pCR = 0.065).
source: Importantly, this temporally precise pattern of consensus building is not present on error trials. On error trials, stimulus consensus dynamics decreased over the course of the trial whereas choice dynamics did not display a systematic increase with the exception of choice non-classically responsive ensembles in AC which remained systematically lower than correct trials (Figure 8F, Δconsensus, correct trials vs. error trials, stimulus: pSNR = 0.007, pSR = 0.065, choice: pCNR = 0.0048, pCR = 0.065 Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided, Δconsensus on error trials, t = 0 to 0.42 s, pSNR = 1.3 × 10−33, t = −1.0 to 0 s, pCNR = 0.032, pCR = 0.14 Wilcoxon test with Bonferroni correction, two-sided).
evidence: Comparison of consensus dynamics between correct and error trials with statistical significance.

claim: Non-classically responsive ensembles in AC and FR2 increased their unsigned consensus until ~750 ms after tone onset on correct trials (Δconsensus, t = 0 to 0.89 s, p=1.7 × 10−5).
source: Using this metric, we found that the unsigned consensus pattern for non-classically responsive ensembles (ensembles with two or more non-classically responsive members) were shared between AC and FR2 – increasing until ~750 ms after tone onset on correct trials (Figure 8G, stimulus-aligned, Δ consensus, t = 0 to 0.89 s, p=1.7 × 10−5 Wilcoxon test, two-sided).
evidence: Unsigned consensus analysis showing temporal dynamics with statistical significance.

claim: Non-classically responsive ensembles in AC and FR2 increased their unsigned consensus immediately before behavioral response on correct trials (Δconsensus, t = −1.0 to 0.0 s, p=0.0011).
source: Non-classically responsive ensembles in AC and FR2 also increased their unsigned consensus immediately before behavioral response (although values in AC were lower overall; Figure 8G, response-aligned, Δconsensus, t = −1.0 to 0.0 s, p=0.0011 Wilcoxon test, two-sided).
evidence: Unsigned consensus analysis showing temporal dynamics relative to behavioral response with statistical significance.

claim: On error trials, unsigned consensus values did not systematically increase (Δconsensus compared to error trials, p=1.9 × 10−9).
source: This pattern of consensus-building was only present on correct trials. On error trials unsigned consensus values did not systematically increase (Figure 8H, Δconsensus compared to error trials, p=1.9 × 10−9 Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided) suggesting that behavioral errors might result from a general lack of consensus between ensemble members.
evidence: Comparison of unsigned consensus dynamics between correct and error trials with statistical significance.

claim: Activity in both AC and FR2 is required for animals to successfully perform the audiomotor frequency recognition task.
source: We first asked if activity in AC or FR2 is required for animals to successfully perform this audiomotor task. We implanted cannulas into AC or FR2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and infused the GABA agonist muscimol bilaterally into AC or FR2, to inactivate either region prior to testing behavioral performance. We found that task performance was impaired if either of these regions was inactivated, although general motor functions, including motivation or ability to feed were not impaired (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; for AC p=0.03; for FR2 p=0.009 Student's paired two-tailed t-test).
evidence: Pharmacological inactivation experiments showing behavioral impairment with statistical significance.

claim: Stimulus decoding performance was independent of receptive field properties including best frequency and tuning curve bandwidth for AC neurons.
source: Stimulus decoding performance was also independent of receptive field properties including best frequency and tuning curve bandwidth for AC neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Analysis showing lack of relationship between decoding performance and receptive field properties.

claim: Neural spike trains from individual units were multiplexed in that they often encoded information about both stimulus category and choice simultaneously.
source: We also observed that task information was distributed across both AC and FR2, and neural spike trains from individual units were multiplexed in that they often encoded information about both stimulus category and choice simultaneously (Figure 4B, Table 1).
evidence: Analysis of decoding performance showing simultaneous encoding of multiple task variables.

claim: Short-term synaptic plasticity and synaptic integration provide powerful mechanisms for differential and specific spike-timing-based coding.
source: We hypothesize that ISI-based decoding is biologically plausible. Short-term synaptic plasticity and synaptic integration provide powerful mechanisms for differential and specific spike-timing-based coding. We illustrated this capacity by making whole-cell recordings from AC neurons in vivo and in brain slices (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), as well as in FR2 brain slices (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). In each case, different cells could have distinct response profiles to the same input pattern, with similar overall rates but different spike timings.
evidence: Whole-cell recordings demonstrating differential responses to identical input patterns.

claim: Different cells can have distinct response profiles to the same input pattern, with similar overall rates but different spike timings.
source: We illustrated this capacity by making whole-cell recordings from AC neurons in vivo and in brain slices (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), as well as in FR2 brain slices (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). In each case, different cells could have distinct response profiles to the same input pattern, with similar overall rates but different spike timings.
evidence: Whole-cell recording data showing variability in spike timing responses.

claim: ISI-based decoding requires few assumptions about implementation and does not require additional separate integrative processes to compute rates or form generative models.
source: Moreover, we note that this type of coding scheme requires few assumptions about implementation, and does not require additional separate integrative processes to compute rates or form generative models. Thus, ISI-based decoding coding could be generally applicable across brain areas, as demonstrated here for AC and FR2.
evidence: Theoretical argument about the computational simplicity of the ISI-based approach.

claim: Tones were 100 ms in duration presented sequentially once every 5–8 s at 70 dB sound pressure level (SPL).
source: Tones were 100 ms in duration presented sequentially once every 5–8 s at 70 dB sound pressure level (SPL); the target tone was 4 kHz and non-target tones ranged from 0.5 to 32 kHz separated by one octave intervals.
evidence: Explicit description of stimulus parameters in the behavioral task.

claim: The fraction of non-classically responsive AC neurons observed is consistent with previous studies that use different auditory stimuli or behavioral paradigms.
source: While the fraction of non-classically responsive AC neurons observed is consistent with previous studies that use different auditory stimuli or behavioral paradigms (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011; Rodgers and DeWeese, 2014), this definition does not preclude the possibility that non-classically responsive cells can be driven by other acoustic stimuli or behavioral paradigms.
evidence: Comparison to previous literature with citations.

claim: The ISI distribution could vary between task conditions even without changes in the firing rate.
source: The ISI was chosen because its distribution could vary between task conditions even without changes in the firing rate – building on previous work demonstrating that the ISI distribution contains complementary information to the firing rate (Lundstrom and Fairhall, 2006; Reich et al., 2000; Zuo et al., 2015).
evidence: Rationale for using ISI with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The observed ISI distributions were better modeled by non-parametric methods rather than standard parametric methods (e.g. rate-modulated Poisson process).
source: We verified that our observed distributions were better modeled by non-parametric methods rather than standard parametric methods (e.g. rate-modulated Poisson process; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparison of model fits showing superiority of non-parametric approach.

claim: The observed ISI distributions are better described by the non-parametric KDE distribution than by rate-modulated Poisson distributions (AC: p=1.1 × 10−15 FR2: p=1.2 × 10−16).
source: Positive values indicate KDE distributions are generically a superior fit for the data (AC: p=1.1 × 10−15 FR2: p=1.2 × 10−16, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of log-likelihood values between KDE and Poisson models.

claim: Achieving a shared ISI representation of task variables may be relevant for successful task execution.
source: The observed increases in ensemble consensus on correct trials (while failing do so on error trials) suggests that achieving a shared ISI representation of task variables may be relevant for successful task execution.
evidence: Inference drawn from the differential consensus dynamics observed on correct versus error trials.

claim: Behavioral errors might result from a general lack of consensus between ensemble members.
source: On error trials unsigned consensus values did not systematically increase (Figure 8H, Δconsensus compared to error trials, p=1.9 × 10−9 Mann-Whitney U test, two-sided) suggesting that behavioral errors might result from a general lack of consensus between ensemble members.
evidence: Comparison of consensus dynamics between correct and error trials leading to inference about error mechanism.

claim: Cells which appear unmodulated during behavior do not encode task information independently, but do so by synchronizing their representation of behavioral variables dynamically during the trial.
source: In summary, we have shown that cells which appear unmodulated during behavior do not encode task information independently, but do so by synchronizing their representation of behavioral variables dynamically during the trial.
evidence: Summary statement integrating findings about consensus dynamics in non-classically responsive cells.

claim: The cortical circuits that generate behavior exist in a distributed network, blurring the traditional modular view of sensory and frontal cortical regions.
source: AC and FR2 each represent both task-variables; furthermore, in both regions, we identified many multiplexed neurons that simultaneously represented the sensory input and the upcoming behavioral choice including non-classically responsive cells. This highlights that the cortical circuits that generate behavior exist in a distributed network – blurring the traditional modular view of sensory and frontal cortical regions.
evidence: Interpretation of findings showing task information distributed across regions.

claim: FR2 is critical for identifying the appropriate sensory-motor association.
source: The prevalence of stimulus information in FR2 might be surprising given that AC reliably responds to pure tones in untrained animals; however, when tones take on behavioral significance, this information is encoded more robustly in frontal cortex, suggesting that this region is critical for identifying the appropriate sensory-motor association.
evidence: Interpretation of finding that FR2 encodes stimulus information better than AC in behavioral context.

claim: Task-relevant stimulus information is reflected more homogeneously in local firing activity across FR2 while this information is reflected in a more complex and distributed manner throughout AC.
source: Furthermore, the stark improvement in stimulus encoding for small ensembles in FR2 suggests that task-relevant stimulus information is reflected more homogeneously in local firing activity across FR2 (perhaps through large-scale ensemble consensus-building) while this information is reflected in a more complex and distributed manner throughout AC.
evidence: Interpretation of ensemble decoding results comparing AC and FR2.

claim: Cholinergic neuromodulation could offer a mechanism for adjusting the sensitivities of resonator networks during behavior on short time-scales by providing rapid phasic signals.
source: In this case, cholinergic neuromodulation could offer a mechanism for adjusting the sensitivities of such a network during behavior on short time-scales by providing rapid phasic signals (Hangya et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanism with citation to supporting literature.

claim: After training, downstream neurons do not need to continually change the readout mechanism; rather, the upstream and downstream components might be modified together by cortical plasticity during initial phases of behavioral training.
source: Thus, after training, downstream neurons do not need to continually change the readout mechanism- rather, the upstream and downstream components might be modified together by cortical plasticity during initial phases of behavioral training. This would set the ISI distributions appropriate for firing of task-relevant downstream neurons, which would ensure that ensemble consensus is reached for correct sensory processing in highly trained animals.
evidence: Speculation about learning mechanism based on findings.

claim: Mechanisms of long-term synaptic plasticity such as spike-timing-dependent plasticity can redistribute synaptic efficacy, essentially changing the dynamics of short-term plasticity independent from overall changes in amplitudes.
source: We additionally hypothesize that mechanisms of long-term synaptic plasticity such as spike-timing-dependent plasticity can redistribute synaptic efficacy, essentially changing the dynamics of short-term plasticity independent from overall changes in amplitudes (Markram and Tsodyks, 1996).
evidence: Hypothesis about plasticity mechanisms with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Downstream neurons may be attuned to the ISIs specified by the consensus LLR of an ensemble.
source: Our consensus results reveal dynamic changes in the relationship between the LLRs of ensemble members. How might such a downstream resonator interpret a given ISI in the context of these dynamics? Our consensus analysis provides one possible answer: downstream neurons may be attuned to the ISIs specified by the consensus LLR of an ensemble.
evidence: Speculation about downstream readout mechanism based on consensus findings.

claim: An ensemble would have the strongest influence on downstream activity when they reach high consensus.
source: In such a model, an ensemble would have the strongest influence on downstream activity when they reach high consensus.
evidence: Inference about functional significance of consensus dynamics.

claim: Single neurons can act as resonators tuned to a certain periodicity of firing input.
source: Furthermore, this is supported by experimental and theoretical work showing that single neurons can act as resonators tuned to a certain periodicity of firing input (Izhikevich, 2000).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Different postsynaptic cells can respond differently to the same input pattern with a fixed overall rate, emphasizing the importance of considering a code sensitive to precise spike-timing perhaps via mechanisms of differential short-term plasticity such as depression and facilitation.
source: Our whole-cell recordings from both AC and FR2 demonstrate that different postsynaptic cells can respond differently to the same input pattern with a fixed overall rate, emphasizing the importance of considering a code sensitive to precise spike-timing perhaps via mechanisms of differential short-term plasticity such as depression and facilitation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data from whole-cell recordings supporting spike-timing-based coding.

claim: The response properties of cortical neurons in a behavioral context become complex in ways that challenge our conventional assumptions.
source: These results underscore the importance of measuring neural activity in behaving animals and using unbiased and generally applicable analytical methods, as the response properties of cortical neurons in a behavioral context become complex in ways that challenge our conventional assumptions (Carcea et al., 2017; Fritz et al., 2010; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017; Otazu et al., 2009).
evidence: General statement about complexity of neural responses with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Non-classically responsive neurons are especially prevalent in frontal cortical regions but can also be found throughout the brain, including primary sensory cortex.
source: These 'non-classically responsive' neurons are especially prevalent in frontal cortical regions but can also be found throughout the brain, including primary sensory cortex (Hromádka et al., 2008; Jaramillo and Zador, 2011; Rodgers and DeWeese, 2014).
evidence: Statement about distribution of non-classically responsive neurons with citations.

claim: Some cells apparently become non-classically responsive during task engagement without impairing behavioral performance.
source: These response categories are not fixed but can be dynamic, with some cells apparently becoming non-classically responsive during task engagement without impairing behavioral performance (Carcea et al., 2017; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017; Otazu et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement about dynamic nature of response categories with citations.

claim: The potential contribution of non-classically responsive cells to behavior remains to a large extent unknown and represents a major conceptual challenge to the field.
source: The potential contribution of these cells to behavior remains to a large extent unknown and represents a major conceptual challenge to the field (Olshausen and Field, 2006).
evidence: Statement about knowledge gap with citation.

claim: Many but not all auditory cortical neurons respond to pure tones with reliable, short-latency phasic responses.
source: Many but not all auditory cortical neurons respond to pure tones with reliable, short-latency phasic responses (Hromádka et al., 2008; Hubel et al., 1959; Kadia and Wang, 2003; Merzenich et al., 1975; Polley et al., 2007; Wehr and Zador, 2003; Yaron et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about AC response properties with multiple citations.

claim: AC neurons can process sound in a dynamic and context-sensitive manner, and AC cells are also modulated by expectation, attention, and reward structure.
source: These neurons can process sound in a dynamic and context-sensitive manner, and AC cells are also modulated by expectation, attention, and reward structure, strongly suggesting that AC responses are important for auditory perception and cognition (David et al., 2012; Fritz et al., 2003; Hubel et al., 1959; Jaramillo and Zador, 2011; Weinberger, 2007).
evidence: Statement about AC function with multiple citations.

claim: FR2 is not thought to be part of the canonical central auditory pathway but is connected to many other cortical regions including AC.
source: In contrast, FR2 is not thought to be part of the canonical central auditory pathway but is connected to many other cortical regions including AC (Nelson and Mooney, 2016; Schneider et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about FR2 anatomy with citations.

claim: FR2 has been shown to be involved in orienting responses, categorization of perceptual stimuli, and in suppressing AC responses during movement.
source: This region has recently been shown to be involved in orienting responses, categorization of perceptual stimuli, and in suppressing AC responses during movement (Erlich et al., 2011; Hanks et al., 2015; Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about FR2 function with citations.

claim: Mixed selectivity cells have been shown to have computational advantages necessary for flexible behavior.
source: Another population of responsive cells are modulated by multiple task parameters ('mixed selectivity cells') and have recently been shown to have computational advantages necessary for flexible behavior (Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about mixed selectivity cells with citation.
